title: Market Failure/ Government intervention to correct Market Failure
outcomes: Define market failure, tell complete from partial market failure, and name its four main sources.

Explain externalities (positive and negative, in production and in consumption), private versus social cost, public goods and the free-rider problem, and information failures — adverse selection and moral hazard.

Describe how governments correct each kind of failure: competition law, direct controls, Pigouvian taxes, cap-and-trade, subsidies, merit and demerit good policies, price floors and ceilings, disclosure rules and redistribution.
Work simple numerical problems on social cost, the socially optimal output, price controls and tradable permits, and recognise government failure.

meta.exam_tip: Expect statement-based MCQs: "adverse selection happens BEFORE the deal, moral hazard AFTER"; "not every good with a negative externality is a demerit good"; "Pigouvian tax = make the polluter pay". Learn the four-cell externality grid with one example each.

concepts.title: Introduction and the concept of market failure
body: Economists assume people act rationally in their own interest. If markets worked perfectly, prices would send correct signals and the right quantity of every good would be produced at the right price. That does not always happen.

Market failure is a situation in which a free market allocates society's scarce resources inefficiently — producing too much or too little of some goods — so the outcome is less than optimal. It does not mean the market has stopped working; it means the market is not working as it should.
Complete market failure ("missing market"): the market supplies nothing at all even though people want the good — for example pure public goods such as national defence.
Partial market failure: the market works but delivers the wrong quantity or charges the wrong price, causing a loss of welfare.
concepts.analogy: A complete failure is a shop that never opens; a partial failure is a shop that opens but stocks the wrong amount at the wrong price.
concepts.work: When a client asks why its industry is heavily regulated (power, telecom, pharma, insurance), the answer usually lies in a specific market failure — natural monopoly, externality or information gap.

concepts.title: Why do markets fail? — and market power
body: Perfect competition (many small firms, perfect knowledge, identical products) would send resources to their highest-valued uses, so that no one can be made better off without making someone worse off. Real markets rarely meet these conditions.
Four major reasons for market failure: (1) market power, (2) externalities, (3) public goods, (4) incomplete information.

Market power (also called monopoly power) means a firm can push its price above marginal cost and still make a profit. A firm with such power is a price maker: it restricts output below the competitive level and charges a higher price. Its profits come from dominance, not efficiency, so society gets too little of the good at too high a price.
concepts.analogy: A single ferry operator on an island can run fewer trips and charge more — not because it is better, but because there is no other boat.
concepts.work: Competition law practice (an area many CAs work in) asks whether a firm's high margins come from efficiency or from abuse of dominance.

concepts.title: Externalities — private cost and social cost
body: An externality is an effect of production or consumption on third parties that is not reflected in market prices. Negative externalities impose costs on others; positive externalities confer benefits. They are also called spillover, neighbourhood, third-party or side effects. Because they bypass the price mechanism, nobody pays or is paid for them — they are uninternalised.
A change that works through prices (for example more people buying organic food pushing its price up) is NOT an externality.

Production externalities: negative, felt in consumption — a factory's effluent makes river water unsafe for families downstream; negative, felt in production — the same effluent reduces fishermen's catch; positive, felt in production — a firm trains workers who later join other firms; positive, felt in consumption — a beautiful private garden enjoyed by passers-by.

Consumption externalities: negative, felt in consumption — smoking in public, a loud music system; negative, felt in production — noisy students disturbing a class, heavy drinking lowering work output; positive, felt in consumption — vaccination protecting others; positive, felt in production — employees using a gym become more productive for the firm.

Private cost is what the firm pays (wages, materials, power) and records in its books; the market supply curve reflects only private marginal cost. Social cost = private cost + external cost. Likewise, social benefit = private benefit + external benefit.

Since prices ignore external costs and benefits, they send wrong signals: goods with negative externalities are over-produced and goods with positive externalities under-produced. That is market failure.

blocks.title: The externality grid

concepts.analogy: A neighbour's barbecue party: the smoke in your window is a cost you did not agree to; the free music you enjoy is a benefit you did not pay for. Neither shows up in his bill.
concepts.work: ESG and BRSR (Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting) work by CAs is largely about measuring and disclosing a company's externalities — emissions, water use, waste.

concepts.title: Public goods and the free-rider problem
body: Paul Samuelson (1954, "The Pure Theory of Public Expenditure") developed the theory of public (collective consumption) goods: goods that all enjoy together, where one person's use does not reduce what is left for others.
Private goods are rival (my eating an apple means you cannot eat it) and excludable (non-payers can be kept out). Markets supply them well — food, clothing, cars, cinema tickets.

Public goods are non-rival (a street light serves every walker equally), non-excludable (once defence is provided, no resident can be shut out), and indivisible (everyone consumes the same total amount). The extra cost of one more user is zero, and no direct payment is made for pure public goods. Examples: national defence, law enforcement, lighthouses, street lighting, public sanitation, disease prevention, basic research.

Free-rider problem: since nobody can be excluded, people have no reason to pay — they can enjoy the good without paying. Profit-seeking firms cannot charge a price, so they produce too little or nothing. This is market failure (often complete).
concepts.analogy: A fireworks show over the city: everyone looks up for free, so no ticket seller can recover the cost — unless the city pays for it.
concepts.work: Public-private partnership projects (toll roads, airports) work only when the "public good" can be made excludable — a toll booth or entry fee lets a private operator recover cost.

concepts.title: Incomplete information — adverse selection and moral hazard
body: Competitive markets assume buyers and sellers know everything relevant. In reality information is incomplete because products are complex (heart surgery, mutual funds), correct information is hard to get, and some parties deliberately mislead (persuasive advertising).
Asymmetric information: one side knows more than the other — landlord vs tenant, borrower vs lender, used-car seller vs buyer, a health-insurance buyer vs the insurer, insiders vs ordinary investors.

Adverse selection arises BEFORE the transaction from hidden information. In health insurance, the insurer cannot tell high-risk from low-risk buyers, so it charges an average premium; high-risk people buy more cover, claims rise, premiums rise, and low-risk people drop out — until mostly unhealthy people remain or the market disappears (a missing market).

Akerlof's "market for lemons": used-car buyers cannot judge quality, so they offer a price based on average quality; owners of good cars withdraw, bad cars ("lemons") dominate, and quality and prices both fall. Asymmetric information drives high-quality goods out.

Moral hazard arises AFTER the transaction from hidden action: a party protected from the full cost of its behaviour takes more risk. A fully insured driver drives carelessly; a fully insured patient does not care about costly treatment. Insurers cannot watch behaviour cheaply, so premiums rise for everyone, and the market may shrink or vanish.
concepts.analogy: Adverse selection: you cannot see inside the melon before buying. Moral hazard: you lent your bike and the borrower rides it carelessly because the repair bill is yours.
concepts.work: Credit appraisal by bank CAs is a fight against both: due diligence and collateral reduce adverse selection; covenants and stock audits reduce moral hazard after the loan is given.

concepts.title: Government's role and intervention to minimise market power
body: A free market still needs the state: physical infrastructure (roads, bridges, airports, waterways), institutional infrastructure (law, regulation, rule of law, property rights, enforcement of contracts) and a suitable competition and consumer law framework.

Against market power India has the Competition Act, 2002 (amended in 2007); the US has antitrust laws and the UK the Competition Act, 1998. They prohibit anti-competitive agreements, cartels, collusion and predatory pricing.

Other measures: opening monopoly sectors to competition (energy, telecom); controls on mergers and acquisitions that may create dominance; price caps and price regulation; profit or rate-of-return regulation; support for consumer associations; investigation of cartels and unfair practices; curbs on monopsony power; lower import controls; and nationalisation.

Sometimes government protects monopoly deliberately — patents and copyrights reward invention. Natural monopolies (electricity, gas, water supply) can supply the whole market at lower cost than several firms; they are allowed but their prices are regulated.
concepts.analogy: The referee does not ban strong players; he stops them from fouling. A patent is a temporary "reserved seat" given as a reward for innovation.
concepts.work: Electricity tariff petitions before regulators are prepared largely by CAs — computing allowed costs and return on equity under rate-of-return regulation of a natural monopoly.

concepts.title: Government intervention to correct externalities
body: Goal: internalise the externality — make those who cause it include the external cost (or benefit) in their own decisions.

Direct controls (command-and-control): emission standards with penalties; licences, production quotas and mandated processes; bans on certain goods; smoking bans in public places; strict rules on tobacco advertising and packaging; environmental laws such as the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986; compulsory pollution-control equipment (which raises firms' average cost, so new firms enter only if price covers cost plus abatement); special bodies such as the Ministry of Environment and the Central and State Pollution Control Boards.

Market-based tools work through prices. (1) Pollution (Pigouvian) tax, after A. C. Pigou — the polluter pays per unit of pollution, raising private cost and cutting output. Problems: hard and costly to measure and administer; weak effect if demand is inelastic (firms pass the tax on); may push firms to relocate to low-tax countries, hurting jobs and investment.

(2) Tradable emission permits (cap-and-trade): the government caps total emissions by issuing a fixed number of permits; firms that cut pollution cheaply sell spare permits, high-cost abaters buy them. Each unit of pollution now has an opportunity cost. The cap fixes the quantity of pollution, and pollution is cut at the least total cost; but firms with inelastic demand can pass on the permit cost. The US used it for sulphur dioxide from 1994.

India has no explicit carbon price, but has implicit ones: the Perform, Achieve and Trade (PAT) scheme, a cess on coal, lignite and peat (replaced in 2017 by the GST compensation cess), Renewable Purchase Obligations and Renewable Energy Certificates, internal carbon pricing; the Energy Conservation (Amendment) Bill, 2022 empowers the Union to set up a carbon credit trading scheme.

Positive externalities lead to under-production, so government gives corrective subsidies to producers (e.g. fertiliser subsidy) or consumers (e.g. subsidised education fees), or produces directly (public education, health care, basic research, afforestation, sewage treatment, cleaning toxic sites).
concepts.analogy: A Pigouvian tax sets the price of pollution and lets the quantity adjust; cap-and-trade sets the quantity of pollution and lets the price adjust.
concepts.work: Companies under PAT or carbon-credit schemes need CAs to account for certificates and permits (as assets, liabilities or inventory) and to verify reported savings.

concepts.title: Merit goods and demerit goods
body: Merit goods have large positive externalities and are socially desirable — education, health care, housing, fire protection, waste management, libraries, museums, parks. Markets can supply them but under-produce and people under-consume them.

Responses: regulation (how education is imparted; compulsory insurance; compulsory immunisation; laws on helmets and seat belts), compulsion (the RTE Act, 2009 makes schooling free and compulsory for ages six to fourteen; compulsory treatment for contagious disease), subsidies, direct provision, provision free at the point of use (free hospital treatment), or a public–private combination.

Demerit goods are socially undesirable — cigarettes, alcohol, intoxicating drugs. Free markets over-produce and over-consume them. Not every good with a negative externality is a demerit good — steel making pollutes but steel is not undesirable.

Responses: outright ban (narcotics); negative advertising campaigns; bans on advertising and promotion; restricting access, especially for children; spatial and time restrictions (no smoking in public places, no tobacco sale near schools, sale banned at certain hours); very high taxes (see the GST rates on tobacco); a minimum price below which the good may not be sold.

Limits: demand for cigarettes and alcohol is usually price-inelastic, so taxes reduce consumption less than proportionately and sellers pass taxes on; total bans often push the trade underground into black markets.
concepts.analogy: Merit goods are vegetables the market under-serves; demerit goods are junk food it over-serves. The government is the parent adjusting the plate.
concepts.work: Excise and GST planning for tobacco and liquor clients — some of the most heavily taxed goods in India — is a specialised practice area for CAs.

concepts.title: Public goods and price intervention (non-market pricing)
body: Direct provision by government overcomes free-riding: defence, the legal system, fire protection and disease prevention are almost always publicly provided.

Excludable public goods (parks, universities, museums) may be financed by entry fees, or a licensed private firm may build them and charge users at a regulated fee. Some are funded by voluntary contributions, corporate donations and NGOs. Some goods that could be private are kept public because profit motives could endanger society — drug approval, atomic energy, airport security.

Price controls are legal limits on prices. A price ceiling (maximum price) is set below equilibrium to keep essentials affordable, e.g. caps on food-grain prices in scarcity or rent control; it creates a shortage (demand exceeds supply), queues and possible black markets.

A price floor (minimum price) is set above equilibrium to protect sellers, e.g. minimum wages and Minimum Support Price (MSP) for crops with government procurement; it creates a surplus that the government may buy.
Buffer stocks: the government buys grain in good harvests and releases it in poor years to keep prices and supply stable.
concepts.analogy: A ceiling is a low roof — the price cannot rise through it, so demand piles up beneath it (shortage). A floor is a raised platform — the price cannot fall below it, so unsold goods pile up on it (surplus).
concepts.work: Food-processing and agri-trading clients must plan for MSP and procurement policies; their CAs model the impact on raw material cost.

concepts.title: Correcting information failure, equitable distribution and government failure
body: Information failure remedies: compulsory accurate labelling and content disclosure (health warnings on cigarettes, nutrition labels on food); mandatory disclosure in financial markets (SEBI requires accurate information to investors in new issues); public information campaigns; regulation of advertising standards.

Equitable distribution: progressive income tax, transfer payments and unemployment benefits, subsidies, targeted spending in the budget, social security, reservation in jobs, land reforms and gender budgeting; also action against the black economy. Interventions that reduce efficiency but increase equity are often justified because society values equity.

Government failure: intervention meant to correct a market failure itself creates inefficiency or misallocation — when it is ineffective and wastes resources, or when it creates new and worse problems. Every intervention has costs and benefits that must be weighed.
concepts.analogy: A doctor who prescribes the wrong medicine can make the patient worse — government failure is the economy's version of a bad prescription.
concepts.work: Audit and disclosure rules (Companies Act, SEBI LODR) exist precisely to fix information asymmetry between managers and investors — the auditor is the economy's information-failure specialist.

illustrations.title: Private cost, external cost and social cost
illustrations.q: A dyeing unit's private cost is ₹400 per metre of cloth. Its effluent causes health and cleaning costs to villagers estimated at ₹60 per metre. It produces 10,000 metres. Find the social cost per metre, total external cost and total social cost. What per-unit tax would internalise the externality?

solution.text: Social cost = private cost + external cost = 400 + 60 = ₹460 per metre. A Pigouvian tax of ₹60 per metre (equal to the marginal external cost) makes the unit bear the full social cost.

illustrations.title: Over-production under a negative externality
illustrations.q: Market demand for a chemical is P = 1000 − 2Q and the industry's private marginal cost (supply) is P = 200 + 2Q. Each unit causes external damage of ₹80. Find (a) the market equilibrium, (b) the socially optimal output and price, (c) the over-production, and (d) the tax revenue if a Pigouvian tax of ₹80 per unit is imposed.

solution.text: (c) Over-production = 200 − 180 = 20 units: the market ignores the ₹80 damage, so too much is produced at too low a price.
(d) With a ₹80 tax, supply becomes 280 + 2Q and output falls to the optimum 180; tax revenue = 80 × 180 = ₹14,400.

checks.label: Pigouvian tax revenue at the optimum

illustrations.title: Price ceiling and price floor
illustrations.q: For a pulse, Qd = 5,000 − 20P and Qs = 1,000 + 20P (Q in quintals, P in ₹ per quintal). Find the equilibrium. What happens if (a) the government fixes a maximum price of ₹80, (b) it fixes a support price of ₹120 and buys any surplus? What does procurement cost?

solution.text: (b) The government must buy the surplus of 800 quintals at ₹120 per quintal, an outlay of 800 × 120 = ₹96,000. A ceiling below equilibrium causes shortages and queues; a floor above it causes surpluses.

illustrations.title: Why cap-and-trade is cheaper
illustrations.q: Firms A and B each emit 100 tonnes. The government wants total emissions cut by 60 tonnes and issues 70 permits to each firm (cap = 140). A can cut emissions at ₹500 a tonne, B at ₹1,200 a tonne. Compare the cost (a) if each firm must cut 30 tonnes itself, (b) if A cuts 60 tonnes and sells its 30 spare permits to B at ₹800 each.

solution.text: With trading A earns 24,000 from selling permits, so its net cost is 30,000 − 24,000 = ₹6,000 (better than ₹15,000). B pays ₹24,000 for permits instead of ₹36,000 of abatement. The same 60 tonnes are cut, but society saves ₹21,000 because the cheaper abater does the cutting.

jobs.title: Pricing a health-insurance product
jobs.role: CA in an insurer's finance and actuarial support team
jobs.situation: Claims on a new no-medical-test policy are far above expectations.
steps: Recognise adverse selection: without tests, high-risk buyers are over-represented.
Propose screening — medical tests above an age, waiting periods for pre-existing illness.
Recognise moral hazard in claims: add co-payment or deductibles so policyholders share costs.
Recompute the premium on the revised risk pool.
jobs.takeaway: Information-failure theory explains real product design choices — waiting periods, co-pay and medical tests.
jobs.think: Which of the two problems does a co-payment clause mainly address?
jobs.answer: Moral hazard — it makes the insured bear part of the cost of their behaviour after the policy is bought.

jobs.title: Carbon credits in the books
jobs.situation: The company exceeded its PAT target and received energy-saving certificates it can sell.
steps: Identify the scheme as a market-based tool that internalises an externality.
Value the certificates and decide whether to sell or hold for future shortfalls.
Disclose the scheme and its impact in sustainability reporting.
jobs.takeaway: Tradable permits turn pollution reduction into a revenue opportunity for efficient firms — exactly the incentive the theory predicts.

jobs.title: Advising a restaurant chain on a price cap
jobs.situation: A city caps the price of a staple meal below the market rate.
steps: Explain that a ceiling below equilibrium creates excess demand — longer queues and pressure on quality.
Estimate the volume increase and cost per plate at the capped price.
Advise on whether to continue the item, reduce portion or seek a subsidy.
jobs.takeaway: Price controls change behaviour on both sides of the market; the business must plan for the shortage they create.

mcqs.q: Market failure means that:
options: The market has stopped functioning completely in every case
The government has failed to collect taxes
mcqs.explain: It is misallocation — over- or under-production — not necessarily a total breakdown.

mcqs.q: When a market does not supply a good at all even though people want it, it is:
mcqs.explain: Pure public goods are the classic case of a missing market.

mcqs.q: Identify the item that is NOT among the four major sources of market failure:
mcqs.explain: The four are market power, externalities, public goods and incomplete information. Perfect competition is the efficient benchmark.

mcqs.q: Market power is best described as the ability of a firm to:
options: Profitably raise price above marginal cost
Produce at the lowest average cost
Sell any quantity at the market price
mcqs.explain: Price-making power lets the firm restrict output and earn profits from dominance.

mcqs.q: A rise in the price of organic vegetables because more people now prefer them is:
options: Not an externality — it works through the price mechanism
mcqs.explain: Effects transmitted through prices are not externalities; externalities are effects outside the price system.

mcqs.q: Effluent from a factory reduces the catch of fishermen downstream. This is a:
options: Negative production externality received in production
Negative consumption externality received in consumption
Negative production externality received in consumption
mcqs.explain: It starts in production (the factory) and harms production (fishing).

mcqs.q: Employees who use a health club become more productive, benefiting their employer. This is a:
options: Positive consumption externality received in production
Positive production externality received in consumption
mcqs.explain: The externality starts in consumption (gym use) and benefits production (the firm).

mcqs.q: Social cost equals:
mcqs.explain: Social cost is the total cost to society: what the firm pays plus what third parties bear.

mcqs.q: A firm's private cost is ₹250 per unit and external cost ₹35 per unit. The social cost per unit is:
mcqs.explain: 250 + 35 = 285. ₹215 subtracts the external cost by mistake.

mcqs.q: Under a negative production externality, a free market tends to:
options: Over-produce the good at too low a price
Under-produce the good at too high a price
mcqs.explain: Firms ignore external cost, so supply is too high and price too low.

mcqs.q: A good that is non-rival and non-excludable is a:
mcqs.explain: Non-rivalry and non-excludability define a pure public good.

mcqs.q: The free-rider problem arises mainly because public goods are:
mcqs.explain: If non-payers cannot be excluded, people have no incentive to pay.

mcqs.q: The concept of the "collective consumption good" was developed by:
mcqs.explain: Samuelson, "The Pure Theory of Public Expenditure", 1954.

mcqs.q: The marginal cost of providing a pure public good to one more user is:
mcqs.explain: One more person under the street light costs nothing extra.

mcqs.q: Only people with high health risks buying insurance, which pushes premiums up and drives healthy people out, illustrates:
mcqs.explain: Hidden information before the contract — adverse selection.

mcqs.q: A person drives carelessly after buying comprehensive motor insurance. This is:
mcqs.explain: Hidden action after the contract — moral hazard.

mcqs.q: Akerlof's "lemons problem" shows that asymmetric information can:
options: Drive high-quality goods out of the market
Raise the average quality of goods
mcqs.explain: Buyers pay for average quality; good-car owners withdraw; lemons remain.

mcqs.q: Which statement is correct?
options: Adverse selection arises before a transaction; moral hazard after it
Moral hazard arises before a transaction; adverse selection after it
Both arise only in public goods
Both are forms of market power
mcqs.explain: Adverse selection = hidden information pre-contract; moral hazard = hidden action post-contract.

mcqs.q: India's main law to promote competition and curb anti-competitive practices is the:
mcqs.explain: The Competition Act, 2002 (amended in 2007).

mcqs.q: Governments allow natural monopolies in electricity and water supply but usually:
options: Force them to sell at zero price
mcqs.explain: One firm supplies most cheaply, so it is allowed, but its price is regulated.

mcqs.q: A tax levied on a polluter equal to the external damage it causes is called a:
mcqs.explain: Named after A. C. Pigou — it makes the polluter pay.

mcqs.q: Which is a limitation of pollution taxes?
options: If demand is inelastic, firms pass on the tax and pollution falls little
They put an absolute cap on pollution
mcqs.explain: Inelastic demand lets firms shift the burden to buyers, so output and pollution fall little.

mcqs.q: Under cap-and-trade, the government directly fixes:
options: The tax rate per unit of pollution
mcqs.explain: The cap sets the quantity; the market sets the permit price.

mcqs.q: Market demand is P = 1000 − 2Q and private supply P = 200 + 2Q. If external cost is ₹80 per unit, the socially optimal output is:
mcqs.explain: 1000 − 2Q = 280 + 2Q → Q = 180. 200 is the market output ignoring the externality; 220 wrongly subtracts the external cost from supply.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT necessarily a demerit good even though it causes a negative externality?
mcqs.explain: Steel production pollutes, but steel is socially useful — not all goods with negative externalities are demerit goods.

mcqs.q: Making education free and compulsory for children aged 6 to 14 is an intervention for a:
mcqs.explain: Education is a merit good; the RTE Act, 2009 compels and subsidises its consumption.

mcqs.q: Heavy taxes on cigarettes may not cut consumption much because:
mcqs.explain: With inelastic demand, quantity falls less than proportionately to a price rise.

mcqs.q: For a good, Qd = 5,000 − 20P and Qs = 1,000 + 20P. If a price ceiling of ₹80 is imposed, the shortage is:
mcqs.explain: Qd = 3,400; Qs = 2,600; shortage = 800. 3,400 and 2,600 are the separate quantities, not the gap.

mcqs.q: Minimum Support Price for crops is an example of a:
mcqs.explain: MSP guarantees farmers a minimum price, above the market price when it binds.

mcqs.q: Mandatory nutrition labels on packaged food mainly correct:
mcqs.explain: Disclosure rules give consumers the information they lack.

mcqs.q: Government failure occurs when:
options: Intervention creates inefficiency or new problems
The government runs a budget surplus
mcqs.explain: An ineffective or harmful intervention misallocates resources further.

questions.q: Demand for cement in a region is P = 900 − 3Q and private marginal cost is P = 100 + Q. Dust from kilns causes external damage of ₹40 per unit. Find (a) market output and price, (b) socially optimal output and price, (c) the over-production, and (d) the Pigouvian tax and its revenue at the optimum.

model.text: (d) Pigouvian tax = marginal external cost = ₹40 per unit; revenue = 40 × 190 = ₹7,600.

scheme.pt: Social marginal cost formed correctly (add external cost)

remarks: Strong answers wrote SMC = PMC + MEC before solving.
mistakes: Subtracting the external cost from supply.
Computing tax revenue at market output instead of optimum output.
tips: State each equation before solving; show the price by substituting back into demand.

questions.q: For wheat, Qd = 12,000 − 50P and Qs = 2,000 + 50P. (a) Find the equilibrium. (b) What happens if a maximum price of ₹85 is fixed? (c) What happens if instead a support price of ₹110 is fixed, and what does it cost the government to buy the surplus?
remarks: Many candidates reversed shortage and surplus.
mistakes: Saying a ceiling causes a surplus.
Valuing procurement at the equilibrium price.

questions.q: Firms X and Y each emit 100 tonnes; total emissions must fall by 80 tonnes. X can abate at ₹300 a tonne and Y at ₹900 a tonne. Each receives 60 permits. Compare total abatement cost if (a) each firm cuts 40 tonnes itself, (b) X cuts 80 tonnes and sells 40 permits to Y at ₹600 each. Show each firm's position.

model.text: X: abatement 24,000 less permit receipts 24,000 = net ₹0 (vs ₹12,000). Y: pays ₹24,000 for permits (vs ₹36,000). Society saves ₹24,000 with the same 80-tonne cut.

scheme.pt: Conclusion: same cut at least cost

remarks: Permit payments are transfers between firms, not a cost to society — the best answers said so.
mistakes: Adding permit payments to society's cost.
tips: Separate society's resource cost (abatement) from transfers (permit sales).

summary: Market failure = inefficient allocation; complete (missing market) or partial (wrong quantity/price).
Four sources: market power, externalities, public goods, incomplete information.
Externality grid: negative/positive × production/consumption, received by producers or consumers. Social cost = private + external cost.
Public goods: non-rival, non-excludable, indivisible, zero marginal cost → free riding → under-provision (Samuelson 1954).
Asymmetric information: adverse selection (before, hidden information; lemons — Akerlof) and moral hazard (after, hidden action).

Remedies: Competition Act 2002; direct controls; Pigouvian tax (price fixed); cap-and-trade (quantity fixed); subsidies; merit/demerit good policies; price ceilings (shortage) and floors (surplus); buffer stocks; disclosure; redistribution.
Government failure: intervention that wastes resources or creates new problems.
remember: India: PAT, coal cess → GST compensation cess (2017), RPO/REC, carbon credit trading under the Energy Conservation (Amendment) Bill 2022.
Not every negative-externality good is a demerit good (steel).
traps: A price change through the market is not an externality.
Ceiling below equilibrium → shortage; floor above → surplus.
Permit payments are transfers, not social cost.

quickref.v: Private cost + external cost (social benefit = private + external benefit)
Set demand = PMC + MEC; Pigouvian tax per unit = MEC
Non-rival + non-excludable (+ indivisible, zero MC) → free rider
Before deal / hidden information vs after deal / hidden action
Ceiling (max) below equilibrium → shortage; floor (min, MSP) above → surplus
Tax fixes the price of pollution; cap fixes its quantity

viva.q: What is market failure, and what are its two types?
viva.model: Market failure is when a free market allocates resources inefficiently, producing too much or too little of some goods. Complete market failure means the market does not supply the good at all, a missing market, as with pure public goods. Partial market failure means the market works but gives the wrong quantity or the wrong price.

viva.q: What are the characteristics of a public good? Why will the market not supply it?
viva.model: A public good is non-rival, so one person's use does not reduce anyone else's, and non-excludable, so non-payers cannot be kept out. It is indivisible and the extra cost of one more user is zero. Because people can enjoy it without paying, they free ride, so private firms cannot charge a price and will not produce it.

viva.q: Distinguish between adverse selection and moral hazard.
viva.model: Adverse selection happens before the transaction because of hidden information, for example only high-risk people buying health insurance or lemons in the used car market. Moral hazard happens after the transaction because of hidden action, for example an insured driver driving carelessly because the insurer bears the loss.

viva.q: Compare a Pigouvian tax with a cap-and-trade system for controlling pollution.
viva.model: A Pigouvian tax charges the polluter per unit of pollution, so it fixes the price of pollution and makes the polluter pay; the quantity of pollution then adjusts. Cap-and-trade fixes the total quantity of pollution through a limited number of permits, and firms trade permits so the price adjusts; the cut is achieved at the least cost because cheap abaters sell permits.

viva.q: How does the government deal with merit goods and with demerit goods? Give examples.
viva.model: Merit goods like education and health care are under-consumed, so the government subsidises them, provides them directly or free, and may make them compulsory, like free and compulsory schooling for children aged six to fourteen. Demerit goods like cigarettes and alcohol are over-consumed, so the government taxes them heavily, bans or restricts them, and bans their advertising.

viva.q: What is the effect of a price ceiling and of a price floor? Give one example of each.
viva.model: A price ceiling is a maximum price set below the equilibrium, for example rent control or capped food prices, and it causes a shortage because demand exceeds supply. A price floor is a minimum price set above the equilibrium, for example minimum support price or minimum wage, and it causes a surplus because supply exceeds demand.

cases.title: The tannery cluster on the river
cases.case: A cluster of tanneries faces demand P = 600 − Q and private marginal cost P = 100 + Q (Q in thousand hides). Effluent harms farmers downstream by ₹50 per thousand hides. The state considers (i) a pollution tax, (ii) issuing a fixed number of tradable effluent permits, or (iii) simply ordering every tannery to install treatment plants.

mcqs.q: What output will the unregulated market produce?
What is the socially optimal output?
mcqs.explain: 600 − Q = 150 + Q → Q = 225. 275 wrongly subtracts the external cost from supply.

mcqs.q: Option (iii), ordering treatment plants, is an example of:
mcqs.explain: It mandates a process rather than working through prices.

mcqs.q: Which statement about options (i) and (ii) is correct?
options: The tax fixes the price of pollution; permits fix its quantity
The tax fixes the quantity; permits fix the price
Both fix the quantity of pollution
mcqs.explain: A Pigouvian tax sets a per-unit price; a cap sets the total emissions allowed.
